metaTitle: Should You Smile in Your LinkedIn Headshot? Yes, Here Is Why
metaDescription: Yes, smile in your LinkedIn headshot. A relaxed, natural smile reads as trustworthy in about 100 milliseconds. When neutral is right, and why forced grins fail.
excerpt: Yes, you should smile in your LinkedIn headshot, as long as it is a natural, relaxed one. Trustworthiness is the first thing people judge from a face, and a positive expression pushes it up. quickAnswer: Yes, smile in your LinkedIn headshot. content:
Yes, smile in your LinkedIn headshot. A natural, relaxed smile, closed or slightly open, is the safest expression for almost every profession, because the first thing a viewer decides about a face is whether they trust it, and a warm expression pushes that judgment in your favour. The exceptions are a handful of roles where gravity is part of the job, and even there a soft, closed-mouth smile usually beats a blank stare.

The rest of this guide covers the research behind that verdict, when a neutral face is the right call, why a forced grin fails, and a simple trick for producing a real smile on cue.

Should you smile in your LinkedIn headshot?

Yes. Todorov and colleagues showed in The functional basis of face evaluation that snap judgments of faces are organised around two axes, trustworthiness and dominance, and that features which resemble a positive expression push a face up the trustworthiness axis. A smile is the most direct way to add those features.

That judgment also happens before anyone reads your headline. Princeton research found people form impressions of trustworthiness, competence and likeability after about 100 milliseconds of exposure, and looking longer mostly makes them more confident rather than changing their mind. Your expression sets the tone for everything on the page below it.

When is a neutral expression the right choice?

When your clients are paying for seriousness. A litigator, a surgeon, a security consultant or a compliance officer is often hired for composure under pressure, and a wide smile can read as lightweight in those contexts. A calm, level expression with soft eyes signals that you are steady and not easily rattled.

Even then, aim for warm neutral rather than stern. Slightly relaxed cheeks and eyes that look engaged keep you on the trustworthy side of the line without tipping into a grin. A hard, unsmiling face scores higher on dominance, which is not the quality most people are looking for in someone they might message cold.

If you are unsure which camp you fall into, look at the profiles of the ten people you most want to be compared with. If most of them are smiling, smile. If most are not, a closed-mouth smile is the safe middle ground.

Why does a forced smile fail?

Because viewers can tell. A genuine smile lifts the cheeks and narrows the eyes a little; a forced one moves the mouth and leaves the eyes flat. The result reads as tense or nervous, which pulls the face toward the anxious end of the trustworthiness axis rather than the warm end.

The forced grin usually comes from holding a smile too long. By the fourth or fifth frame of a photographer saying "big smile", the muscles have locked and the expression has drained out. Short bursts beat long holds: relax completely, then bring the smile back fresh for each shot.

The other common failure is over-doing it. A full, teeth-baring laugh is great in a wedding album and slightly manic at thumbnail size beside a comment. Stop at the point where the smile feels comfortable, not at the point where it feels maximal.

How do you get a real smile on cue?

Use the "someone you like walked in" trick. Just before the shutter, imagine a friend or colleague you genuinely enjoy walking through the door behind the camera. Your face will respond the way it does in real life: a small lift in the cheeks, a softening around the eyes, a smile that arrives rather than one you assemble.

A few other things help:

  • Exhale slowly before each frame so the jaw and shoulders drop.
  • Look slightly above the lens for a beat, then back at it, to reset the eyes.
  • Take far more frames than you think you need and pick the one where the eyes are doing the work.
  • Keep the chin level; tilting it up reads as challenge, tilting it too far down reads as sheepish.

If you are shooting selfies for an AI set, the same rules apply, and they matter more. The model learns your face from what you upload, so a batch of stiff selfies produces stiff headshots.

Yes, and this is where an AI set has a real advantage over a single photographer session. faqs.question: Should I smile with teeth in my LinkedIn headshot?
faqs.answer: Either works, so choose what feels natural. A slightly open smile reads warmest and most approachable, while a closed-mouth smile reads calm and composed. The one to avoid is a wide, teeth-baring laugh, which looks manic at thumbnail size, so stop where the smile feels comfortable rather than where it feels biggest.

faqs.question: Is it unprofessional to smile in a LinkedIn photo?
faqs.answer: No. For most professions a relaxed smile is the expected default, and research on face evaluation shows positive expressions raise perceived trustworthiness, the first thing viewers judge. The only fields where a neutral face can be better are those hired for gravity, such as some legal, medical and security roles.

faqs.question: How do I stop my smile looking fake in photos?
faqs.answer: Do not hold it: relax fully between frames, then think of someone you like walking into the room just before the shot so the smile arrives on its own. A real smile lifts the cheeks and narrows the eyes, while a fake one moves only the mouth. Take many frames and pick by the eyes.

faqs.question: Can an AI headshot generator make me smile if my selfies are neutral?
faqs.answer: Partly, but results are far better when your input covers both. Picturesk trains a model on the 5 to 15 selfies you upload, so include a few with an easy smile and a few neutral. That gives the model real examples of both expressions and the finished set will contain convincing versions of each.
